AS: Culture and lifestyle

5 missions. Guess, learn, then check. Your place is saved.

  1. Mission 1France tried to keep under-15s off social media in 2026. What stopped it, and who is right?
  2. Mission 2Teenagers in France smoke far less than they did a few years ago. What changed, and what risks remain?
  3. Mission 3Why must French radio stations play a set share of songs in French, and does it still matter?

Mission 1

Mission 1: France tried to keep under-15s off social media in 2026. What stopped it, and who is right?

Make a guess: France tried to keep under-15s off social media in 2026. What stopped it, and who is right?

Mission 1

Who are the cybernauts?

  • Un(e) cybernaute / un(e) internaute – an internet user.
  • Baromètre du numérique 2026 (people aged 12+, surveyed in 2025):
  • 91% own a smartphone.
  • 86% have a home internet subscription; 86% use instant messaging.
  • 48% use generative AI, up 15 points in one year.
  • But not everyone is connected: l'illectronisme – lacking the skills or the access to use the internet. INSEE: 15.4% of people aged 15+ in 2021, mostly older people and people on low incomes.
  • la fracture numérique – the digital divide
  • être connecté(e) – to be online · un écran – a screen · une appli(cation) – an app
Mission 1

How technology makes daily life easier

  • Public services online (les démarches en ligne): tax returns, ID applications, benefits.
  • Health: booking a doctor online; video consultations (la téléconsultation).
  • Work and study: le télétravail; online school platforms (e.g. Pronote) for marks, homework and messages to parents.
  • Money: mobile banking, contactless payment.
  • Staying in touch: messaging and video calls with family far away.
  • Grâce à Internet, on gagne du temps. – Thanks to the internet, we save time.
  • Tout est à portée de main. – Everything is within reach.
  • Watch out: grâce à (thanks to, positive) vs à cause de (because of, negative).
Quick check
?Ma grand-mère est en situation d'illectronisme. What does this mean?
Mission 1

The dangers

  • Le cyberharcèlement – online harassment. A criminal offence in France. Young victims can call 3018, a free national helpline.
  • Les infox / les fausses informations – fake news; la désinformation.
  • La dépendance aux écrans – screen addiction; effects on sleep, attention and mood are widely debated.
  • Les données personnelles – personal data. The EU's GDPR (le RGPD) sets rules; the CNIL enforces them in France.
  • Les arnaques en ligne – online scams, e.g. l'hameçonnage (phishing); l'usurpation d'identité – identity theft.
  • Les discours de haine – hate speech; illegal content can be reported on the state platform Pharos.
  • signaler un contenu – to report content · protéger sa vie privée – to protect one's privacy
Mission 1

Protecting young people: the 2026 law

  • 2018: phones banned in écoles and collèges.
  • 2023: a law sets a "digital majority" at 15 (parental consent for younger users). It never came into force.
  • 2026: Parliament votes to ban social media for under-15s, with age checks for all users.
  • 14 August 2026: the Conseil constitutionnel strikes the ban down. It finds it a disproportionate limit on freedom of expression and communication, and says the compulsory age checks lacked safeguards for privacy.
  • 24 August 2026: the rest of the law is promulgated. Phones are now banned in lycées too (from September 2026), and schools must teach about screen risks.
  • The government says it is aiming for a new framework by spring 2027.
  • le Conseil constitutionnel censure la loi – strikes down the law · promulguer – to sign into law
Quick check
?Which statement about the 2026 law is accurate?
Mission 1

Vocabulary bank

  • la cyber-société – the cyber-society
  • les réseaux sociaux – social media
  • naviguer sur Internet – to browse the internet
  • télécharger – to download
  • un mot de passe – a password
  • la vie privée – privacy
  • une infox – a piece of fake news
  • l'intelligence artificielle (IA) – artificial intelligence
  • un algorithme – an algorithm
  • la vérification de l'âge – age verification
  • la liberté d'expression – freedom of expression
  • l'éducation aux médias – media literacy
Mission 1

Faut-il interdire les réseaux sociaux aux moins de 15 ans ? Argue both sides

  • Arguments made by supporters of a ban:
  • Les réseaux sociaux nuisent au sommeil et à la santé mentale des adolescents. – Social media harm teenagers' sleep and mental health.
  • Les plateformes sont conçues pour capter l'attention. – Platforms are designed to capture attention.
  • Les parents ne peuvent pas tout contrôler seuls. – Parents cannot control everything on their own.
  • Arguments made by opponents:
  • Une interdiction générale porte atteinte à la liberté d'expression. – A general ban harms freedom of expression.
  • Vérifier l'âge de tous les utilisateurs menace la vie privée. – Checking every user's age threatens privacy.
  • Mieux vaut éduquer qu'interdire. – Better to educate than to ban.
  • Balance: La question n'est pas seulement de savoir s'il faut interdire, mais comment protéger. – The question is not only whether to ban, but how to protect.
Quick check
?Choose the best French for: "If social media were banned, young people would find other ways."
Mission 1

Model sentences and exam tasks

  • Il faut que les plateformes protègent davantage les mineurs. (il faut que + subjunctive)
  • Bien qu'Internet nous facilite la vie, il nous rend parfois dépendants. (bien que + subjunctive; rendre + adjective)
  • Ce que les jeunes craignent le plus, c'est d'être exclus du groupe. (cleft for emphasis)
  • Unit AS 1 presentation (3 min) on social media and new technology, then conversation (about 8 min).
Mission check

?Which statement about digital life in France is accurate?

Give a figure, a danger, a benefit, and the 2026 law as a case study, with both sides. That is what examiners reward.

Mission 2

Mission 2: Teenagers in France smoke far less than they did a few years ago. What changed, and what risks remain?

Make a guess: Teenagers in France smoke far less than they did a few years ago. What changed, and what risks remain?

Mission 2

How healthy are 17-year-olds?

  • The ESCAPAD survey (OFDT) questions 17-year-olds across France.
  • Daily smoking: 25.1% in 2017 → 15.6% in 2022.
  • Has tried cannabis: 39.1% → 29.9%. Regular cannabis use: 7.2% → 3.8%.
  • Alcohol: of those who drank in the last month, 36.6% had at least one heavy session (une alcoolisation ponctuelle importante, binge drinking).
  • Trend: most risky behaviours are falling, but binge drinking is still common.
  • le tabagisme – smoking (as a habit) · une enquête – a survey · la consommation – use, consumption · en baisse / en hausse – falling / rising
Mission 2

Why do young people take risks?

  • Reasons often given: curiosity, the group, stress, the search for thrills, feeling invincible.
  • Risk is not only drugs: dangerous driving, extreme sports, online challenges.
  • les sports extrêmes – extreme sports · le saut à l'élastique – bungee jumping · le parapente – paragliding
  • Some risks are chosen and prepared (training, equipment); others are suffered (addiction).
  • une conduite à risque – risky behaviour · la dépendance – addiction, dependence · se sentir invincible – to feel invincible
  • Watch out: risquer de + infinitive = to be likely to (something bad): Tu risques de te blesser – You could hurt yourself.
Quick check
?En 2022, 15,6 % des jeunes de 17 ans fumaient tous les jours, contre 25,1 % en 2017. Which summary is accurate?
Mission 2

What the state does: prevention laws

  • 1991: loi Évin: strict limits on advertising for tobacco and alcohol.
  • 2007–2008: smoking banned in enclosed public places, then in cafés and restaurants.
  • 2009: sale of tobacco and alcohol to under-18s banned.
  • 2017: plain packaging for cigarettes (le paquet neutre).
  • 2025: disposable e-cigarettes (les puffs) banned.
  • 29 June 2025: smoking banned on beaches, in parks, at bus shelters and near schools; fine €135.
  • la prévention – prevention · interdire – to ban · une amende – a fine · un fumeur / une fumeuse – a smoker
Mission 2

Diet and nutrition

  • Le repas gastronomique des Français (sitting down together, several courses) is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list (2010).
  • Nutri-Score (since 2017): a label from A (green) to E (red) on the front of food packs. It is voluntary for brands.
  • 2016: large supermarkets must give unsold food that is still edible to charities instead of destroying it.
  • Debates: la malbouffe (junk food), sugar in drinks, organic food, eating meat.
  • l'équilibre alimentaire – a balanced diet · grignoter – to snack · le gaspillage alimentaire – food waste · bio – organic (invariable: des produits bio)
Quick check
?Choose the best French for: "Young people are drinking less and less alcohol."
Mission 2

Stress and mental health

  • Pressure points for students: exams (le bac), choosing a course on Parcoursup, social media, the future.
  • Mental health was France's grande cause nationale for 2025, extended to 2026.
  • Mon soutien psy: up to 12 sessions a year with a psychologist, reimbursed by health insurance.
  • Help lines: 3114 (suicide prevention, 24/7) · Fil Santé Jeunes (for 12–25s).
  • la santé mentale – mental health · le mal-être – unhappiness, distress · être stressé(e) · l'anxiété (f) · demander de l'aide – to ask for help
  • Watch out: Je suis stressée (a girl speaking) agrees; le stress is a masculine noun.
Mission 2

Managing well-being

  • Physical activity: since 2022, primary schools must give 30 minutes of physical activity every day.
  • After Paris 2024, debate about turning the Olympic interest into regular sport for young people.
  • Sleep: screens late at night cut sleep; teenagers need more sleep than adults.
  • Balance: l'équilibre entre vie professionnelle et vie privée – work–life balance; leisure, relaxation, time with friends.
  • se détendre – to relax · faire du sport · bien dormir · déconnecter – to switch off (from screens)
  • Plus on dort mal, plus on a du mal à gérer le stress. – The worse you sleep, the harder stress is to manage.
Mission 2

Argue both sides

  • Should the state protect people from themselves?
  • Yes (arguments supporters make):
  • La prévention sauve des vies. – Prevention saves lives.
  • Les maladies liées au tabac coûtent cher à la collectivité. – Illnesses linked to tobacco cost society a lot.
  • No (arguments supporters make):
  • Chaque adulte doit rester libre de ses choix. – Every adult must stay free to make their own choices.
  • Trop d'interdictions rendent le risque plus attirant. – Too many bans make risk more attractive.
  • Linkers: Il est vrai que … ; toutefois … · Les partisans de … estiment que … · En revanche …
  • Your turn: "The more you ban, the more young people want to try."
    Show answer

    Plus on interdit, plus les jeunes ont envie d'essayer.

Quick check
?Depuis le 29 juin 2025, il est interdit de fumer sur les plages. What does this mean?
Mission 2

Vocabulary, model sentences and exam tasks

  • le tabagisme · une conduite à risque · la dépendance · la prévention · une amende · la malbouffe · l'équilibre alimentaire · le gaspillage alimentaire · la santé mentale · le mal-être · le sommeil · se détendre
  • Il faut que l'État agisse avant que les jeunes ne commencent à fumer. (il faut que, avant que + subjunctive; ne here is optional and not negative)
  • Bien que les jeunes fument de moins en moins, l'alcool reste un risque important. (bien que + subjunctive)
  • AS Unit 1: 3-minute presentation, then about 8 minutes of conversation. Angle: Le stress des examens : comment le gérer ? Use one figure from the earlier screen.
Mission check

?Which statement about health policy in France is accurate?

In a health essay, one precise figure and one law are worth more than a paragraph of general advice.

Mission 3

Mission 3: Why must French radio stations play a set share of songs in French, and does it still matter?

Make a guess: Why must French radio stations play a set share of songs in French, and does it still matter?

Mission 3

One language, many musics

  • La musique francophone: music in French, or by artists from French-speaking countries and communities.
  • France: chanson, rap, electronic music (la French touch).
  • Belgium: Stromae, Angèle. Québec: Céline Dion.
  • Caribbean: zouk (Kassav', from Guadeloupe and Martinique).
  • West and Central Africa: mbalax (Youssou N'Dour, Senegal), zouglou and coupé-décalé (Côte d'Ivoire), Congolese rumba, on UNESCO's intangible heritage list since 2021.
  • Many artists mix French with other languages: Wolof, Lingala, Creole, Arabic, English.
  • un genre musical · un(e) artiste · un tube – a hit · mêler – to mix
Mission 3

Changes and developments

  • 1940s–60s: la chanson à texte: the words matter most (Édith Piaf, Georges Brassens, Jacques Brel).
  • 1960s: les yé-yé: pop for teenagers, inspired by British and American rock (Johnny Hallyday, Françoise Hardy).
  • 1980s–90s: rap arrives and grows fast (MC Solaar, IAM, NTM).
  • Late 1990s: la French touch: French electronic music known worldwide (Daft Punk, Air).
  • 2010s–today: streaming; rap becomes the dominant genre; more women at the top (Aya Nakamura, Angèle).
  • évoluer – to evolve · s'inspirer de – to draw on · un courant – a movement
Quick check
?Which statement about francophone music is accurate?
Mission 3

Who listens, and how?

  • France's recorded music market: €1.07 billion in 2025, growing for ten years (SNEP).
  • Streaming is now the main way to listen: about 165 billion streams in 2025.
  • Vinyl is back: almost 6 million records sold in 2025.
  • French music is strong at home: 16 of the 20 best-selling albums of 2025 were French productions.
  • Young listeners: mainly streaming and short videos. Older listeners: more radio and CDs.
  • écouter en streaming · un abonnement – a subscription · télécharger – to download · un auditeur / une auditrice – a listener · le vinyle
Mission 3

Music's impact on popular culture

  • Language: rap spreads new words and expressions into everyday speech.
  • Fashion and image: streetwear, music videos (les clips), artists as brands.
  • National moments: at the Paris 2024 Olympic opening ceremony, Aya Nakamura (born in Mali) performed with the band of the Garde républicaine, and Céline Dion sang Édith Piaf's L'Hymne à l'amour from the Eiffel Tower.
  • La Fête de la musique (21 June, since 1982): free concerts in the streets, now copied in many countries.
  • Debates: who represents France? Should a national event reflect today's popular music?
  • un chanteur / une chanteuse · se produire – to perform · rassembler – to bring together
Quick check
?Les radios doivent diffuser au moins 40 % de chansons d'expression française. What does this mean?
Mission 3

How to safeguard francophone music

  • Radio quotas (law of 1994, in force 1996): music radio must play at least 40% French-language songs, half of them by new talents or new releases.
  • Quotas apply to radio, not to streaming platforms.
  • Le Centre national de la musique (CNM, 2020): public body that supports artists, venues and producers.
  • Festivals and prizes: Les Francofolies (La Rochelle, since 1985), les Victoires de la musique (since 1985).
  • Schools and local venues: music education, salles de concert, the Fête de la musique.
  • sauvegarder – to safeguard · soutenir – to support · diffuser – to broadcast · un quota
  • Your turn: "Without quotas, radio stations would play fewer French songs."
    Show answer

    Sans quotas, les radios diffuseraient moins de chansons françaises.

Mission 3

Argue both sides

  • Are radio quotas still useful?
  • Yes (arguments supporters make):
  • Les quotas aident les jeunes artistes à se faire connaître. – Quotas help young artists get known.
  • Sans eux, les radios passeraient surtout des tubes anglo-saxons. – Without them, radio would mostly play English-language hits.
  • No (arguments supporters make):
  • À l'ère du streaming, les quotas ont perdu leur sens. – In the streaming age, quotas have lost their point.
  • Imposer une langue limite la liberté artistique. – Imposing a language limits artistic freedom.
  • And English? Some French artists sing in English to reach the world (Daft Punk); others say French is part of their identity.
  • Linkers: Certes …, mais … · Il n'en reste pas moins que … · Selon ses défenseurs, …
Quick check
?Complete: « C'est une chanteuse ___ tout le monde parle. »
Mission 3

Talking about a song without quoting it

  • In exams, describe and analyse in your own words.
  • Dans cette chanson, l'artiste évoque … – In this song, the artist evokes …
  • Les paroles dénoncent / célèbrent … – The lyrics criticise / celebrate …
  • Le refrain répète une idée, ce qui souligne … – The chorus repeats an idea, which highlights …
  • Le rythme est lent / rapide ; la mélodie est … · Le clip montre … – The video shows …
  • les paroles (f pl) – lyrics · un couplet – a verse · le refrain – the chorus · rendre hommage à – to pay tribute to
  • Watch out: les paroles is plural: les paroles sont touchantes. Une parole alone means a word or a promise.
Mission 3

Vocabulary, model sentences and exam tasks

  • un genre musical · un tube · la chanson à texte · le rap · le streaming · un auditeur / une auditrice · diffuser · un quota · sauvegarder · se produire · les paroles · le refrain
  • C'est une artiste dont les chansons mêlent le français, l'argot et des mots d'autres langues. (dont)
  • Bien que le streaming domine, le vinyle connaît un retour en force. (bien que + subjunctive)
  • Si les radios n'étaient pas obligées de diffuser des chansons en français, les jeunes talents auraient plus de mal à percer. (si + imperfect → conditional)
  • AS Unit 1: 3-minute presentation, then about 8 minutes of conversation. Angle: La place de la musique dans la vie des jeunes.
Mission check

?Which statement is accurate?

Name artists and countries, give one date and one figure, and weigh the quotas. That turns a music answer into an argument.

Mission 4

Mission 4: The first paid film screening was in Paris in 1895. Why do the French call cinema the seventh art?

Make a guess: The first paid film screening was in Paris in 1895. Why do the French call cinema the seventh art?

Mission 4

Why "the seventh art"?

  • 28 December 1895: the Lumière brothers hold the first public, paid film screening, in a room of the Grand Café in Paris.
  • In the 1910s–20s the critic Ricciotto Canudo (an Italian living in Paris) argued that cinema was a full art form.
  • His list: architecture, sculpture, painting, music, dance, poetry, then cinema, the seventh, because it combines them all (space, image, movement, sound, story).
  • Le septième art has been a common French name for cinema ever since.
  • un film · un long-métrage – a feature film · un court-métrage – a short film · le grand écran – the big screen
  • Watch out: un réalisateur / une réalisatrice = a film director. Un directeur runs a company or a school.
Mission 4

Evolution: the main stages

  • 1902: Georges Méliès, Le Voyage dans la Lune: special effects and fantasy.
  • 1930s: poetic realism and Jean Renoir (La Grande Illusion, 1937).
  • 1946: creation of the CNC (state film body) and the first Cannes festival.
  • 1959–60s: la Nouvelle Vague.
  • 1976: the first César awards, France's film prizes.
  • 2000s–2010s: huge popular comedies: Bienvenue chez les Ch'tis (2008) and Intouchables (2011) each sold close to 20 million tickets.
  • 2023: Justine Triet's Anatomie d'une chute wins the Palme d'or (then an Oscar for its screenplay in 2024).
  • Today: streaming platforms alongside cinemas.
Quick check
?Which of these came first?
Mission 4

La Nouvelle Vague

  • Late 1950s–1960s: young critics from the magazine Les Cahiers du cinéma start making films.
  • Key films: Les Quatre Cents Coups (François Truffaut, 1959) · À bout de souffle (Jean-Luc Godard, 1960) · Cléo de 5 à 7 (Agnès Varda, 1962).
  • What was new:
  • filming outdoors, in real streets, with natural light;
  • light, hand-held cameras and small budgets;
  • young, unknown actors;
  • jump cuts and breaking the rules of continuity;
  • the director as auteur: the film expresses one person's vision.
  • le tournage – filming, the shoot · tourner un film – to shoot a film · un(e) cinéaste – a film-maker · une caméra – a film camera
Mission 4

A national passion?

  • France is Europe's largest cinema market (CNC).
  • 2024: 181.5 million tickets sold; French films took 44.7% of them.
  • 2025: 156.8 million tickets (−13.6%); French films 37.7%, American films 35.8%.
  • Cinemas everywhere: from multiplexes to small cinémas d'art et d'essai (independent cinemas showing arthouse films).
  • Cannes each May: the world's best-known film festival.
  • la fréquentation – attendance · les entrées (f) – tickets sold, admissions · une salle (de cinéma) – a cinema, a screen · un(e) cinéphile – a film lover
  • en version originale (VO) – in the original language · en version française (VF) – dubbed into French (doublé) · sous-titré – subtitled
Quick check
?Hier soir, j'ai assisté à l'avant-première du film. What does this mean?
Mission 4

How France funds its cinema

  • L'exception culturelle: the idea that films are culture, not just goods, so the state may protect them (defended by France in world trade talks in 1993).
  • A tax on every cinema ticket goes to the CNC, which reinvests it in French films and cinemas.
  • L'avance sur recettes (since 1959): CNC loans for films chosen for their quality, often first films.
  • TV channels, and since 2021 streaming platforms, must invest part of their revenue in French and European works.
  • La chronologie des médias: rules on how long a film waits after its cinema release before it can be shown on pay TV, streaming, then free TV.
  • financer – to fund · une subvention – a subsidy · un producteur / une productrice · la sortie en salle – cinema release
Mission 4

Cinema in young people's lives

  • Competition: streaming platforms, series, short videos, games.
  • Why young people still go: a social outing, big releases on the big screen, special events (premieres, festivals).
  • What holds them back: ticket prices, films available soon on platforms.
  • Help: discount prices for young people; the pass Culture (a state credit for young people) can be spent on cinema tickets.
  • School screenings: many pupils discover French films through school programmes.
  • une plateforme de streaming · une série · une sortie – an outing; a release · le prix des places – ticket prices
Mission 4

Argue both sides

  • Do cinemas have a future?
  • Yes (arguments supporters make):
  • Voir un film en salle reste une expérience collective unique. – Seeing a film in a cinema remains a unique shared experience.
  • Les grands films sortent d'abord au cinéma. – Major films are released in cinemas first.
  • No, or not as before (arguments supporters make):
  • Les plateformes offrent un choix immense pour le prix d'une place. – Platforms offer a huge choice for the price of one ticket.
  • Le prix des places décourage les familles et les jeunes. – Ticket prices put off families and young people.
  • And state funding? Supporters: it keeps French and arthouse films alive. Critics: it funds films few people see.
  • Your turn: "Although streaming is convenient, nothing replaces the big screen."
    Show answer

    Bien que le streaming soit pratique, rien ne remplace le grand écran.

Quick check
?En 2025, la fréquentation des salles a baissé de 13,6 %. What does this mean?
Mission 4

Vocabulary, model sentences and exam tasks

  • le septième art · un réalisateur / une réalisatrice · un(e) cinéaste · le tournage · un long-métrage · la fréquentation · les entrées · une avant-première · en VO / doublé / sous-titré · l'exception culturelle · une subvention · la sortie en salle
  • Ce qui distingue la Nouvelle Vague, c'est sa liberté : tournage en extérieur, caméra légère et jeunes acteurs.
  • Bien que la fréquentation ait baissé en 2025, la France reste le premier marché du cinéma en Europe. (bien que + perfect subjunctive)
  • Si le CNC ne finançait pas les premiers films, beaucoup de jeunes réalisateurs ne pourraient pas tourner. (si + imperfect → conditional)
  • AS Unit 1: 3-minute presentation, then about 8 minutes of conversation. Angle: Le cinéma français: pourquoi le soutenir ? Set-film essay.
Mission check

?Which statement about French cinema is accurate?

Link history (dates, the Nouvelle Vague) to today (figures, funding, streaming). Examiners reward that "then and now" range.

Mission 5

Mission 5: Why do the French hide a charm in a January cake, and which traditions now divide them?

Make a guess: Why do the French hide a charm in a January cake, and which traditions now divide them?

Mission 5

The French calendar

  • France has 11 public holidays (les jours fériés).
  • Six are Christian in origin: Easter Monday, Ascension, Whit Monday, 15 August, 1 November (la Toussaint), Christmas. A secular Republic kept its Catholic calendar.
  • Others are civic: 1 May (la fête du Travail), 8 May and 11 November (end of the two World Wars), 14 July, 1 January.
  • 14 July (le 14 Juillet): national day by a law of 1880. It recalls the storming of the Bastille (1789) and the Fête de la Fédération (1790).
  • On the day: military parade on the Champs-Élysées, fireworks (le feu d'artifice), firefighters' dances (les bals des pompiers).
  • Watch out: un jour férié – a public holiday; faire le pont – to take the extra day off between a holiday and the weekend.
Mission 5

Customs through the year

  • January, Epiphany: la galette des rois. A small charm (la fève) is hidden inside; whoever finds it is king or queen and wears the paper crown.
  • 2 February, la Chandeleur: people make crêpes.
  • 1 April: le poisson d'avril – children stick paper fish on people's backs.
  • 1 May: people give lily of the valley (le muguet) for luck.
  • 21 June: la Fête de la musique (since 1982): free concerts in the streets.
  • 1 November: families put chrysanthemums on graves.
  • 24–25 December: le réveillon (late Christmas Eve meal), la bûche de Noël – the Yule log cake.
  • Your turn: "At Candlemas, we make pancakes."
    Show answer

    À la Chandeleur, on fait des crêpes.

Quick check
?Which pair is correct?
Mission 5

Festivals across the French-speaking world

  • Québec: la Fête nationale du Québec on 24 June (la Saint-Jean-Baptiste); le Carnaval de Québec every winter since 1955, with its snowman mascot Bonhomme Carnaval.
  • Belgium: the Carnival of Binche – the Gilles dance in wax masks and throw oranges; recognised by UNESCO in 2003.
  • Switzerland: la fête de l'Escalade, Geneva (December), recalls the failed attack on the city in 1602; children smash a chocolate marmite.
  • Martinique and Guadeloupe: carnival ends on Ash Wednesday when Vaval, the carnival king figure, is burned.
  • Senegal: la Tabaski (Eid al-Adha): families gather, sacrifice and share a sheep, and wear new clothes.
Mission 5

The big cultural festivals

  • Le Festival de Cannes (since 1946, May): cinema; top prize la Palme d'or.
  • Le Festival d'Avignon (since 1947, July): theatre; founded by Jean Vilar.
  • La Fête des Lumières (Lyon, around 8 December): in 1852 people lit candles in their windows; today light shows draw huge crowds.
  • Le Carnaval de Nice (February): parades of giant figures and la bataille de fleurs – the flower battle.
  • La Fête de la musique: created by the Ministry of Culture in 1982; copied in many countries.
  • Model: Ce qui me plaît dans la Fête de la musique, c'est qu'elle est gratuite et ouverte à tous.
Quick check
?Which sentence is correct French?
Mission 5

When traditions meet laïcité

  • France's laïcité: the state is neutral towards religions.
  • Question: can a town hall display a Christmas crib (une crèche de Noël)?
  • Conseil d'État, 9 November 2016:
  • in a building housing a public authority (e.g. a town hall): not allowed, unless special circumstances give it a cultural, artistic or festive character (e.g. a local tradition);
  • in other public places (a street, a market): allowed in the Christmas period, if it does not promote a religion.
  • Some see cribs as heritage (le patrimoine, Provençal santons); others as a religious symbol that a neutral state should not display.
  • Watch out: la laïcité ≠ "laity"; it means the separation of religion and state.
Mission 5

Faut-il préserver toutes les traditions ? Argue both sides

  • Case: bullfighting (la corrida), legal only where there is an "unbroken local tradition" (parts of the south). A 2022 bill to ban it was withdrawn before it came to a vote.
  • Keep it (arguments supporters make):
  • La corrida fait partie de l'identité de certaines régions du Sud. – Bullfighting is part of the identity of some southern regions.
  • Elle fait vivre des villes entières pendant les ferias. – It supports whole towns during the ferias.
  • Ban it (arguments supporters make):
  • Une tradition ne justifie pas la souffrance d'un animal. – A tradition does not justify an animal's suffering.
  • Les traditions évoluent : on peut fêter une région sans mise à mort. – Traditions change: a region can celebrate without a killing.
  • Linkers: Au nom de la tradition, … · Pour les uns …, pour les autres … · Tout dépend de …
  • Your turn: "For some it is an art; for others it is cruelty."
    Show answer

    Pour les uns, c'est un art ; pour les autres, c'est de la cruauté.

Mission 5

Vocabulary bank and model sentences

  • une fête – a celebration, festival · un jour férié · une coutume – a custom · célébrer / fêter · un défilé – a parade · le feu d'artifice · un char – a float · se déguiser – to dress up · une tradition qui se perd – a dying tradition · le patrimoine immatériel – intangible heritage · la marchandisation – commercialisation · transmettre – to hand down
  • Même si la pratique religieuse recule, beaucoup de fêtes religieuses restent des moments familiaux.
  • Si les fêtes locales disparaissaient, une partie de l'identité régionale disparaîtrait avec elles. (si + imperfect → conditional)
  • Ce qui rend une fête vivante, c'est qu'elle se transmet d'une génération à l'autre. (cleft for emphasis)
Mission 5

Exam tasks

  • AS 1 presentation (about 3 min) on an aspect of a French-speaking country, e.g. the Carnaval de Québec; then the conversation (about 8 min). At A2, festivals or traditions can be the "Culture" research option.

Recap

The big ideas

Mission 1

  • Cybernauts: 91% own a smartphone; 48% use generative AI; illectronisme 15.4% (2021).
  • Benefits: online public services, health, work, staying in touch. Dangers: cyberharcèlement (3018), infox, addiction, data, scams.
  • 2026: under-15 social-media ban struck down (14 August: freedom of expression, privacy); phones banned in lycées from September 2026.

Mission 2

  • 17-year-olds (ESCAPAD 2022): daily smoking 15.6% (25.1% in 2017); cannabis down; binge drinking still common.
  • Prevention: loi Évin 1991 → indoor bans 2007–08 → 18 minimum age 2009 → plain packs 2017 → outdoor bans 2025.
  • Mental health: national cause 2025–2026; Mon soutien psy (12 sessions); 3114.

Mission 3

  • Diversity: France, Belgium, Québec, the Caribbean, West and Central Africa; many languages mixed with French.
  • Change: chanson → yé-yé → rap → French touch → streaming era (rap dominant; 16 of the top 20 albums of 2025 French).
  • Safeguarding: radio quotas (1994: 40% in French), CNM (2020), festivals, Fête de la musique (1982).

Mission 4

  • Le septième art: Canudo's name for cinema, which combines the other six arts; first paid screening, Paris, 1895.
  • Stages: Méliès (1902) → Renoir → CNC and Cannes (1946) → Nouvelle Vague (1959–60s) → Césars (1976) → popular comedies → streaming.
  • Passion and protection: 181.5 m tickets (2024), 156.8 m (2025); exception culturelle, ticket tax, CNC.

Mission 5

  • 11 public holidays; 14 July national day since 1880; customs: galette des rois, Chandeleur, muguet, Fête de la musique (1982).
  • Francophone festivals: Québec (24 June, winter carnival), Binche, l'Escalade, Antilles carnival, Tabaski.
  • Debates: cribs and laïcité (Conseil d'État 2016); bullfighting, tradition or cruelty.
